newsitem.title: UK: United News drops after HTV deal.
newsitem.headline: United News drops after HTV deal.

text.p: Shares in United News & Media Plc dropped on Monday on concerns the broadcast and newspaper group may have overpaid for HTV, analysts said.

"They will have to make about 10 million (stg) of cost savings to make the deal earnings neutral in the first full year," said one analyst. "The market thinks they will be hard pushed to do that," he added.
United News shares fell 10p to 704.5p by 0950 GMT.
The company announced on Friday it had agreed to take over Wales and west of England broadcaster HTV in a deal valuing HTV at 371 million stg.
United offered 420p per share for HTV and immediately lifted its stake in the company from just under 30 percent to a controlling 51 percent.
HTV shares, which had soared 82.5p on Friday, dipped 2.5p to 412.5p on Monday morning.

Elsewhere in the media sector, Yorkshire-Tyne Tees Television fell five pence to 11.35 stg. Hotels-to-television group Granada has offered 11.75 stg per share for Yorkshire, valuing the company at 711 million stg.

Shares in satellite broadcaster BSkyB Plc continued to hurtle towards earth, falling a further 12p to 441.5p on a newspaper report highlighting a potential threat to its revenues from a review of how pay channels are sold.
BSkyB is hovering near 12 month lows after losing 28 percent of its value over the past two weeks or so following the loss of key executives and an equity stake in digital terrestrial TV.
The Financial Times noted at the weekend that United's bid equated to 40 times last year's earnings while Granada was offering only 32 times.
However, analysts noted compelling commercial reasons for the United bid, which fits well with the company's existing ITV franchises in southern and eastern England.
They also pointed to HTV's strong natural history programming as a complement to United's own output in this area.
United has a stake of around 13 percent in Yorkshire-Tyne Tees. Its move for HTV effectively rules it out as a counter bidder for Yorkshire-Tyne Tees.
Institutional investor Mercury Asset Management, which owns some five percent of Yorkshire, has voiced concern that the Granada bid was pitched too low.

BSkyB shares were unsettled by the report in the Guardian suggesting that the ITC television watchdog could outlaw the "bundling" of channels. This is the practice whereby subscribers have to take combinations of basic and premium channels.
Analysts said the hint of further bad news was enough to push BSkyB shares lower, given their current weakness.
